title: The Sun and Nuclear Fusion
seo_title: Sun Worksheets: Nuclear Fusion, Layers, Life Span and Sunspots (High School Earth Science)
standard_text: Develop a model based on evidence to illustrate the life span of the sun and the role of nuclear fusion in the sun's core to release energy that eventually reaches Earth in the form of radiation.
meta_desc: Free high school Earth and space science worksheets on the Sun (NGSS HS-ESS1-1): nuclear fusion, E = mc², layers of the Sun, star life spans and the sunspot cycle. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Hydrogen fuses into helium in the core; the energy reaches Earth as light.
body_html:
How to think about it

The Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core.

  • Fusion turns a little mass into a lot of energy (E = mc²). Energy moves out through the radiative and convection zones and leaves as light.
  • The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and halfway through its ~10-billion-year main-sequence life.
  • More massive stars fuse faster and have much shorter lives.
Example

1 g of mass converted. Energy?

0.001 × (3 × 108)²

Answer: 9.00 × 1013 J

Example

Sunlight to Earth (150 million km)?

1.5 × 1011 ÷ 3 × 108 = 500 s

Answer: about 8.3 minutes

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the Sun burns like a fire.
  • Confusing fusion (joining) with fission (splitting).
  • Thinking massive stars live longer.

faq.q: How does the Sun make energy?
faq.a: In its core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium. A small amount of mass becomes a large amount of energy (E = mc²).

faq.q: How long will the Sun last?
faq.a: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and will keep fusing hydrogen for about 5 billion more years before becoming a red giant.

faq.q: Why do massive stars have shorter lives?
faq.a: Their cores are hotter and denser, so they fuse hydrogen much faster and run out sooner.
